title: Day 1 Baseline — AWS Staff/Principal Calibration
description: A cold baseline across architecture, Terraform state, incident response, postmortems, disaster recovery, and event systems. Complete without reading the model answers first.
rules: Record audio or video externally if possible.
Keep the initial response between 60 and 120 seconds.
Answer each follow-up directly instead of returning to a memorized speech.
Separate production experience from hypothetical architecture.
Do not guess an AWS quota or unsupported personal metric.

questions.title: Multi-AZ EKS at hyperscale
questions.prompt: Design a highly available Amazon EKS platform for two million concurrent users. The application must tolerate one Availability Zone failure without violating its user-facing SLO.
followups: What additional workload numbers do you need before you can size the platform?
One AZ fails while the other two are already at 80% utilization. What happens?
HPA requests 500 additional pods, but the remaining subnets have insufficient pod IPs. How do you respond?
Why not deploy one extremely large EKS cluster?
What evidence would justify the claim that the platform supports this scale?
must_cover: concurrency translated into requests, bytes, and active connections
AZ and cluster or cell failure domains
pod and node scaling as separate control loops
subnet IPs, quotas, dependencies, and warm capacity
full-path load test including AZ evacuation
unsafe_signals: EKS is managed, therefore the application is highly available

questions.title: Terraform state across accounts and Regions
questions.prompt: Design Terraform state management for a multi-account, multi-Region AWS estate used by many engineering teams.
followups: Why not use one state file for the entire production estate?
The CI job is gone but the state remains locked. When may you force-unlock it?
An S3 replica in another Region contains an older state object. Can it become the active backend automatically?
AWS created a resource, but Terraform timed out before recording it. What is your recovery sequence?
How do consumers obtain outputs without broad access to sensitive state?
must_cover: state treated as a privileged control-plane database
one writer per state and protected short-lived CI identity
state segmentation by blast radius and lifecycle
versioning, encryption, audit, and tested recovery
configuration, state, and AWS reality reconciliation
unsafe_signals: use lock=false during an urgent change
restore the oldest or newest object without checking lineage and reality

questions.title: Route 53-to-application outage
questions.prompt: Customers report that they cannot access an application hosted on AWS. Walk through your investigation and mitigation approach.
followups: Route 53 is healthy. Why can users still fail?
All Application Load Balancer targets are healthy. What does that not prove?
VPC Reachability Analyzer reports the path as reachable, but requests still time out. What next?
Only IPv6 clients and one geographic cohort fail.
Would you restart the application pods?
must_cover: customer impact and one UTC incident timeline
capture of one real failing transaction
outside-in request path from resolver through dependency and response
hypothesis and boundary-specific evidence
smallest reversible mitigation and external recovery proof
unsafe_signals: component health equated with business transaction health

questions.title: Large-outage postmortem
questions.prompt: A global deployment caused a 50-minute customer outage. Describe how you would lead the postmortem and ensure the failure class does not recur.
followups: A junior engineer initiated the deployment. What is the root cause?
Who owns the postmortem?
Leadership asks for the engineer's name in the executive summary.
The review produces 35 corrective actions. How do you prioritize them?
When may the postmortem be considered complete?
must_cover: customer and business impact
fact-based UTC timeline
trigger separated from contributing and safeguard failures
blameless but accountable ownership
corrective actions with owners, dates, risk, and acceptance tests
unsafe_signals: human error as the complete root cause
postmortem complete when the document is published
large unprioritized action list without verification

questions.title: Multi-Region disaster recovery
questions.prompt: Design a multi-Region AWS disaster-recovery strategy with a five-minute RTO and a write RPO below ten seconds.
followups: A single Route 53 health check fails. Should traffic move immediately?
The secondary Region has only 25% of normal compute capacity.
Aurora replication lag is six seconds when the primary Region becomes unreachable.
The old Region might still accept writes through an internal path.
The old Region returns after 20 minutes. Should you fail back immediately?
must_cover: RTO and RPO by capability
independently operable regional cells
destination readiness and capacity realization
source fencing before write-authority promotion
canary traffic shift, reconciliation, restored redundancy, and planned failback
unsafe_signals: DNS described as the complete DR design
automated failover from one noisy signal

questions.title: Millions of events per second
questions.prompt: Design an AWS platform that processes five million real-time events per second using the appropriate combination of Kinesis, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Lambda, and EKS.
followups: The average event size is 1 KB. What does that imply before protocol and replication overhead?
One customer generates 40% of traffic and strict per-customer ordering is required.
A consumer is six hours behind.
One event permanently crashes the consumer.
Lambda scales quickly and overwhelms DynamoDB. What control is missing?
How do you achieve exactly-once business effect?
must_cover: events per second and bytes per second
partition key derived from ordering requirement
distinct roles for Kinesis, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Lambda, EKS, and S3
idempotency, checkpointing, retry ownership, and poison-event handling
backpressure, replay, consumer lag, and end-to-end freshness
unsafe_signals: decorative chaining of every AWS service
random key suffix that violates required ordering
